This study examines the effectiveness of restricting individual messaging in WhatsApp to prevent the spread of inaccurate information. We found that limiting in-app communication to individual contacts rather than groups makes it possible to detect and remove shared content from groups, enabling fact-checkers to verify and stop the spread of false information. However, limiting in-app communication hampers users from easily sharing official information and makes it difficult for fact-checkers to verify content, ultimately reducing the overall impact on the spread of inaccurate information.

We analyze a broad class of population models, including those with sex, for which finite type allelic frequency distributions can be precisely calculated at discrete time steps. This is achieved for a general class of irreducible Markov chains, and specifically for all supercritical population models with a finite type class. Furthermore, precise asymptotic approximations are derived for large, fixed-time frequency distributions and frequency distributions with large sample sizes in supercritical population models of a finite type.

A novel variant of the EER minimizer is presented, specifically designed for spoofing detection countermeasures. The proposed mechanism incorporates an attention module, and an objective function is developed to encourage it to activate distinct regions of the spectrogram, and counterpart generator to produce spectrograms with analogous activated spectrogram areas. Extensive experiments are conducted on the AM-SRC dataset. The results show that the proposed method successfully minimizes EER at lower signal-to-noise ratios compared to a standard setup with no mechanism, and that it minimizes EER at better signal-to-noance ratios compared to other spoofing detection countermeasures.

In this analysis, we explore the constraints imposed on supersymmetric inflationary effective field theories (SFT-EFTs) derived from a global supersymmetry model. By linking SU(2) doublet Higgs superfields to the inflaton within both MSSM-like and U(1) hypercharge-unbroken setups, we identify the conditions under which the inflaton can be separated from the heavy supersymmetric sectors, thus validly employing EFT methods. Furthermore, we trace the potential origins of these models within supersymmetric grand unified theories and examine their implications for post-inflationary reheating and the characteristics of superpartners following the inflationary period.

Parametric down-conversion, a nonlinear process, produces pairs of photons when there is no difference in their spatial properties but there are differences in their spectral properties. However, at the single-photon level, the space-spectrum correlation isn't symmetric. This study investigates how measuring the total photon number from a spectral point source in one daughter photon affects the emitted photon pairs. It shows that the effect of measurement on the signal is not just dependent on the pump intensity, but also on the ratio of the signal to the idler bandwidth.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For developing qubits, cooper-pair box transmon remains the most widely utilized system. However, co-planar waveguide (CPW) resonators are crucial in creating split ring resonators and other spin-based quantum systems. While CPW-based qubits have been operational, the impact of the coaxial cavity on the quantum state remains uncertain. This study investigates the microenvironment of CPW and SRR resonators using a terahertz near-field microscope, with the capability to distinguish between electric and magnetic field components. Our findings show that electromagnetic modes in resonators are confined to the end-caps, contradicting conventional assumptions. These discoveries could guide the design of quantum devices, providing insights into engineering coherent states and  Purcell-enhanced spin-emitters.

Given an arbitrary non-empty collection $\mathcal{U}$ of subsets of the real line $\mathbb{R}$, we investigate under what conditions it is possible to divide $\mathbb{R}$ into disjoint sets, such that each set contains at most one element from every set in $\mathcal{U}$. It is demonstrated that if the collection $\mathcal{U}$ consists of sets that are Borel measurable, then this division is indeed feasible. Furthermore, if the collection $\mathcal{U}$ satisfies a certain topological constraint, we investigate feasible upper bounds for the number of elements in each set that it may contain.

In recent years, advancements in data and computational capabilities have enabled the rise of sophisticated trading techniques like high-frequency and algorithmic trading. Some studies have explored the impact of these strategies through theoretical and practical analyses, yet their broader consequences remain uncertain. This paper employs agent-based modeling to assess the effect of a trading regime characterized by substantial information processing capabilities on market stability, uncovering both positive and negative outcomes, which vary based on the initial distribution of trading strategies.

Identifying network security traffic is crucial for detecting potential threats, yet conventional methods relying on packet signature matching are susceptible to manipulation by attackers who modify their software signatures. To mitigate this drawback, a collaborative approach among security monitoring tools has been proposed, utilizing a distributed system that verifies and shares identifiers among various platforms. Although this technique offers a viable solution, existing implementations have not been thoroughly evaluated, nor have they been tested against attempted evasion strategies. In response to this need, a comprehensive analysis of open-source network security tools was conducted, focusing on their resilience in identifying assault traffic, and also assessing their overall functionality to provide a comprehensive understanding of their reliability in detecting potential threats.

Closed-loop magnon circuits with superconducting proximity effects can isolate and separate topological edge states carrying both electrical and magnetic signals. We investigated this phenomenon by building and studying the edge state of a topological insulator between two others, with one being a normal metal and the other a superconductor. Our findings reveal that the magnetic signal is heavily blocked when passing through the superconducting proximity metal, in contrast to the normal metal. Furthermore, the magnetic signal behaves as if it's unaffected when the geometric shape of the superconducting metal is changed. These results confirm that the edge state responsible for the magnetic signal is indeed influenced by the superconducting proximity effect and show that GSU-based devices have the potential for developing advanced spintronic applications.

A prominent approach in automatic audio recognition is using supervised learning with pre-trained models, although these models, typically based on large datasets like AudioSet, are often outdated and may not be accessible. Additionally, the process of collecting, labeling, and updating data is labor-intensive. Another challenge arises from the decentralized nature of the data, requiring the use of Federated Learning (FL) to avoid transferring data from various sources. We propose ZSFL, a new method combining ZSFL and FL that allows for learning from audio events not present in the training data and events distributed across multiple devices. In this research, we evaluate ZSFL on the AudioEvents2020, freeSound, and GitHub datasets. ZSFL is shown to outperform existing methods in general-classification accuracy and a newly developed metric, zero-shot performance, while also reducing the communication requirements in the FL process by up to 20 times.

There have been various methods to measure Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states in multiple dimensions, such as using maximum sets of mutually unbiased bases or performing ion-trap experiments, but these approaches require precise preparation experiments. Our new proposal offers a universal GHZ state measurement that accommodates arbitrary inputs and is particularly useful when precise preparation experiments are impractical. This protocol measures GHZ states in multiple dimensions by employing joint measurements of generalized Pauli operators at the level of quantum logic circuits. The required operations can be achieved using linear optics, generalized Pauli gates, and post-selection. Our approach has been successfully demonstrated with photons and is shown to expand to cluster states of any graph.

A recent innovation in wireless communication, known as intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS), has shown promise in improving the efficiency of radio frequency communication. However, the complexity of the cascaded channel in an IRS-assisted system poses a challenge in terms of accurate channel estimation. Our work addresses this challenge by proposing a new estimation technique based on sparse recovery. The proposed method treats the cascaded channel as a high-dimensional sparse signal and uses an IRS codebook to generate pilot signals. Our simulation results show that it only requires a low number of pilot symbols to achieve accurate channel estimation. When compared to a conventional estimation method, our technique demonstrates a significant improvement in terms of the information rate by over 2 dB in a system with 10 reflecting elements.

This study examines how U.S. local news outlets responded to the COVID-19 pandemic. The researchers analyzed over 900 million news stories from April 2020 to March 2021, using machine learning to track changes in news content and identify popular themes. The investigation also explores whether news content and audience engagement patterns vary based on the pandemic's stage in different geographic areas and the level of concern for COVID in those regions, as measured by local news sentiment. The results indicate that news content shifted significantly with each phase of the pandemic, and that news outlets in regions with more severe pandemic conditions or high national concern tended to cover the virus more extensively. Upon introduction of vaccines, news content became more optimistic and focused on national trends less so. The study also found that news outlets' focus on national trends and sentiment influenced their audience interaction, and that these micro-level news patterns aligned with, but were also informative beyond, the macro-level national pandemic dynamics.

This study investigates the progression of learning to count through simulations of
neural networks, where the goal is to produce sequential outputs based on a single
input. To achieve this, we developed an architecture utilizing Recurrent Neural Networks
augmented with External Auto-Associative Neural Fields, allowing the system to condition
its learning on previously generated states. By gradually eliminating this external
storage, we observed the effect on the final counting sequences. Our research reveals
that small delays in signal transmission can lead to the self-organization of counting
cycles in the absence of explicit loop structures, providing insight into the early
stages of numerical development. Additionally, we found that the choice of weight update
rules significantly impacts both cyclicity and the accuracy of counting.

Bloom filters are widely used probabilistic data structures for checking element membership, but they can mistakenly identify elements as present when they are not. A variant called the Bloom filter with counting buckets addresses this issue, albeit at the cost of increased memory usage. Another improvement, the cuckoo filter, was developed to offer faster and more efficient membership checks, although it uses a fixed number of hashes per element. This limitation can be a drawback in dynamic environments where the dataset is expected to change over time. A new approach called the XOR filter overcomes these issues by using a Bloom filter with counting buckets and a variable number of hashes per element added and removed as needed. This simplifies add, remove, and space usage in comparison to both the standard Bloom filter and the Bloom filter with counting buckets, while maintaining slightly higher memory usage than cuckoo filters.

We establish a connection between two areas of mathematics, namely convex bodies and algebraic varieties, and analyze how they relate to each other. Specifically, we explore how transformations of convex bodies and alomorphisms of complex spaces correspond, and we demonstrate that certain key properties, such as Blaschke geometry and Einstein metrics, are reflected in this relationship. Additionally, this connection reveals that hermitian Einstein cycles with negative holomorphic sectional curvature are associated with almor spaces.

Traditional price-based models assume that the futures market reflects past and present values, but future trends are unknown. Our research presents a new approach that directly uses execution prices, times of trades, and share volumes to create a framework independent of future trends. This approach transforms the original data into "market directional data," enabling us to build a comprehensive model that includes futures without relying on them. Our study validates this market directional framework by ensuring it adheres to fundamental principles, such as the impossibility of risk-free profit without inside information and consistency with the law of large numbers. Additionally, we show that price-based models derived using this market directional framework等价于 those using futures, but are derived independently of the futures market.

Federated learning (FL) offers a privacy-preserving approach for training a shared model across multiple devices while keeping local data out of the loop. A key limitation in this process is that sensitive information can still be inferred from model parameters. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel framework called FLVoogd, which integrates a differential privacy (DP) mechanism into FL to prevent such inference. By combining FL with FLVoogd, we can achieve a balance between model utility and data confidentiality. Our framework is tested on two widely used datasets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in preventing malicious attacks and safeguarding user privacy.

We examine the challenge of deploying control policies in autonomous driving from simulation to the real world. Our goal is to bridge the gap between synthetic and real-world data distribution by leveraging the forward pass of a convolutional neural network (CNN) to generate target images, which are then used to train a control policy. Our proposed approach relies on minimum-reconstruction error without requiring a reverse pass, making it suitable for end-to-end autonomous driving tasks. We validate our method on the autonomous driving task and compare it to other Sim2Real bridge techniques. Since our proposed method can be applied to task-specific architectures, we also investigate its effectiveness in end-to-end autonomous driving scenarios. Our results show that using reconstruction error can improve the robustness of a pre-trained network and facilitate the transfer of policies from simulation to the real world.

A counterfactual media generation technique, known as deepfake, poses a threat to media authenticity.  Despite its widespread application in the entertainment and news sectors, deepfake images and videos are susceptible to attacks and manipulation.  To overcome these challenges, this research aims to develop a robust deepfake generation and detection system.  The proposed system involves creating a new, resilient deepfake generation method called the Spatially Separable Adversarial Network (SSAN), which can combine multiple images or videos seamlessly.  SSAN achieves this through a process that separates spatial information from feature extraction, allowing it to effectively handle large-scale deepfake video generation.  Furthermore, SSAN's design allows it to generate deepfake media that is compatible with various media types.  To counterattack resilient deepfake media, a new detection approach called the Feature-Matching Aggregation Network (FMAN) is introduced.  FMAN can identify deepfake content in short videos or within longer video content by matching and aggregating features effectively.  The research findings demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy and reliability.

The orbits of sub-Neptune exoplanets around cooler stars can reveal valuable information about their atmospheres, particularly their oceans, through various chemical signatures. These chemical indicators can be explained by the balance of dissolved minerals in the ocean and their subsequent release as the planet evolves. To verify this theory, we employed a model that considers both abiotic mineral dissolution and gas-phase chemistry, taking into account factors such as the planet's temperature, the pressure at which it separates into distinct layers, and its overall mass. Our analysis shows that within a specific temperature range, the dissolved ocean water and salt content can significantly affect the light that the planet emits, and this is further influenced by the pressure-temperature relationship within the planet. Additionally, the water and salt content can also have a notable impact on the light that the planet reflects, and this is particularly evident in cases of high-pressure and salt content. These findings suggest that the mass and internal composition of certain exoplanets, such as GJ 3576 d and K2-22 b, can be better understood, and that more precise data from upcoming telescopes can provide even more in-depth insights.

Recent breakthroughs in sequential tasks using recurrent neural networks have led researchers to translate them into spiking neural networks. In this work, we create a foundational framework for teaching basic sequence tasks using a small number of neurons, driven by unsupervised learning principles. The framework utilizes only unsupervised learning rules, including temporal coding principles. Our results show that these tasks can be successfully completed within the given constraints, marking a significant advancement in creating spiking neural networks capable of learning sequences on their own.

This document serves as the official report for the Out-of-Catalog Image
Recognition (OOCR) challenge, which was held in conjunction with the Vision
and Language Learning (VLL) workshop at EMNTE 2022. The report outlines the
problem addressed in the OOCR task, along with a detailed description of the
dataset and evaluation methodology employed. The report also summarizes the
findings of the participant teams who submitted their solutions for the OOCR
challenge.

A new approach combines adaptive generalized polynomial chaos expansions with robust post-processing techniques to handle complex stochastic problems efficiently and reliably. The framework verifies uPCE representations of solution approximations with controlled error for semi-linear and linear PDEs with uncertainties in parameters and boundary conditions. The error is partitioned into three components: truncation, projection, and quadrature, with the truncation error being minimized through an adaptive uPCE. The method is demonstrated on two and three-dimensional Poisson problems with highly irregular random fields.

This paper addresses the challenging issue of monitoring a complex system with some observable components, focusing on detecting and isolating anomalies in the unobservable remaining parts. We develop an advanced algorithm utilizing Bayesian inference and probabilistic logic to not only identify and isolate the point of change (PC) for the detectable system parts but also deduce the PC for the non-observable parts. Our approach employs dynamic node re-ranking and adaptive time-window adjustment to achieve this goal, supported by our novel system of anomaly logic. We validate our algorithm using a fault-tolerant magnetic bearing system, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling anomalies that occur at distinct time points for both the observable and unobservable system parts.

Dwarf galaxies, especially those destroyed and now in the process of being accreted, can be found in various stages of disruption. Their remains can be identified through their effect on the host galaxy's light and through their external halos. These galaxies offer valuable insights into their past, as their small size allows their entire star creation history and nuclear fusion processes to be fully captured in their remaining light. Their low metal content also makes their light easier to study in detail with high-resolution spectra. This research focuses on two specific examples: Draco and Segue 1. Their small number of stars, around 50,000 stars for Draco, allow for more accurate and comprehensive studies of their galaxy formation and the evolution of their stars.

Given a profinite group $G$, an action spectrum is a specific type of topological space. This space, denoted as $L(G)$, consists of free and transitive $G$-sets. The space $L(G)$ features a continuous action by $G$ in the sense of profinite topology. An action spectrum is also characterized by a system of action spectra corresponding to the subgroups of $G$.

A major challenge with AI-based document understanding solutions is obtaining a large, high-quality training dataset. This work addresses the issue by proposing a method to significantly lower labeling costs for documents with visual elements. It achieves this by using data labeling as a continuous process, where previously labeled data is used to improve less extensively labeled data. A semi-supervised model, enhanced with co-training, further improves the model's performance on fully unlabeled data, all while maintaining minimal to no labeling requirements. Experiments on four IR extraction datasets demonstrate that this approach yields comparable results to using a fully labeled dataset, with a significant reduction in labeling costs.

The EuS/InAs interface has garnered significant interest due to its potential for observing the magneto-electric effect. A comprehensive first-principles study was conducted to investigate the electronic structure and magnetic properties of different EuS/InAs interface configurations. The study focused on two distinct linkages: S-InAs (A) and Eu-InAs (B). The results of density of states and charge density analysis indicated that the S-InAs (A) configuration exhibits an insulating interface, whereas the Eu-InAs (B) configuration displays metallic characteristics, exhibiting spin-orbit splitting in InAs due to charge transfer from Eu. Additionally, the study found that the Eu magnetic moments at the interface in the EuS monolayer exhibit a finite value of 6.86 $\mu_B$. The results of magnetic total energy and interface energy calculations further revealed that the EuS growth on InAs exhibits two stable metal-semiconductor phase coexistence, with a finite Eu magnetic moment in the metallic InAs.

A detailed classification of certain subsets of Baire space, specifically those related to Borel analysis, has been determined through the calculation of Wadge degrees of specific sets. By building on Chong and Li's work, the authors provide a proof for the Wadge degrees of Borel sets, effectively demonstrating $A\times W$ is reducible to $B$ implies $A$ is reducible to $B$ times a countable set. This breakthrough allows for the derivation of $A\times\mathbb{N}$ (or $\mathbb{Q}$) equivalence to $B$. While related results have been obtained for analytical sets, the current findings close the existing gap in Borel analysis.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated exceptional results in a range of machine learning tasks, but high computational costs associated with training these models often hinder adoption, especially for resource-limited settings. To address the problem of DNN training efficiency, we developed ClickTrain, a system that makes DNN training faster and more precise while preserving the network's underlying structure. ClickTrain employs a novel approach that incorporates fine-grained pruning and data-dependent operations to preserve the original architecture of the network during training. This allows ClickTrain to achieve superior model performance and prediction accuracy compared to traditional training methods. ClickTrain also offers two-fold efficiency improvements over these methods: it reduces the computational load during training and accelerates the process by pre-loading data in advance. As a result, ClickTrain outperforms existing methods on image classification, sequence-to-sequence modeling, and ranking tasks, achieving a 1.4 to 7.1 times speedup and producing models with higher prediction accuracy and better performance scores.

This study investigates modal extensions of non-commutative linguistics based on ordered monoids, specifically focusing on the underlying order structure in the development of new logical systems for capturing spatial reasoning. We expand upon an existing logical framework and demonstrate its computational efficiency through sound and complete proof search procedures, specifically for a completed system and a restricted subset. These results build on previous work on the complete Lambek calculus, with a significant contribution being the application to a more complex modal system.

The merging of neutron stars with black holes produces ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, offering a new way to explore the universe. Although the LIGO and Virgo detectors have successfully identified the signals from binary black hole and binary neutron star mergers, the detection of gravitational waves from merging neutron stars with black holes has not been achieved. To improve the understanding of these rare events, new machine learning techniques have emerged that can distinguish between the signals from neutron star-black hole mergers and other types of mergers with greater accuracy. In this research, we demonstrate the effectiveness of a deep learning model in classifying the gravitational waves from these mergers, outperforming traditional methods.

A comprehensive study of a newly discovered transiting exoplanet, TOI-5542b, is presented.  Using a combination of TESS, JWST, and Gaia data, the star's properties of effective temperature, surface gravity, metallicity, age, mass, radius, and distance, are accurately determined.  TOI-5542 is an ancient, cool, and metal-deficient G-type star with a mass of 0.94, and TOI-5542b is a warm Jupiter with a 12.7-day orbital period and 1.2-Jupiter mass.  Notably, TOI-5542b is the first known warm Jupiter detected in the extensive Kepler and TESS datasets, and it shares similarities with Jupiter itself, despite orbiting a metal-poor host star.  The discovery of TOI-5542b is significant as it sheds light on the formation and evolution of gas giant planets, and the statistical analysis of its system dynamics is also explored.

A constrained Markov decision process is optimised for its best possible value function while adhering to specific constraints on another value function. This complex problem is resolved by an algorithm based on the augmented Lagrangian, which is further simplified and simplified. The algorithm is shown to converge and an alternative method is also proposed with potential for a faster convergence rate. The relationship between this approach and other established methods, such as Lagrange multipliers and duality gaps, is also explored.

Math is a fundamental skill that underpins scientific and technical understanding.
 Mathematics education begins in primary school, where students learn various mathematical concepts.
 Recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions is a challenging task due to variations in student handwriting.
 This research presents an advanced method for recognizing mathematical expressions offline, using high-speed,
 low-cost, and easily accessible Raspberry Pi-based systems. The proposed system uses deep learning,
 specifically convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks with bidirectional sequences,
 and attention-based decoding to accurately recognize complex mathematical expressions. The method outperforms
 previous offline mathematical expression recognition systems, achieving a character-level error rate of 19.6%.
 The proposed system is designed to recognize expressions quickly, allowing for real-time performance on a Raspberry Pi.

We observe that in one-dimensional supersymmetric quantum mechanics with superpotential $W$, the shape of $W$ has a profound impact on the supercharge cohomology, $H^*(Q)$. The long-standing assumption that $H^k(Q)$ is non-zero only for odd $k$ when there are no classical local minima is challenged. It is discovered that introducing a singular point, specifically an essential singularity, can result in an infinite sequence of non-trivial odd supercharge cohomology groups. This phenomenon is explored using an elliptic integral and we demonstrate how the Riemann surface structure of such integrals dictates the topological properties of $H^*(Q)$. The connection to the TQFT elliptic genus is also noted, with a key distinction being the absence of a non-trivial elliptic point under the modular group $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$.

To investigate interactions within meta-populations of self-sustaining units on arbitrary network structures, we developed a new analytical framework that creates a complete probability distribution of temporal intervals between non-local variations in population units across the network. This distribution depends on two fundamental characteristics of the system: the underlying network structure and the specific variation measurement chosen. We applied this method to three different types of population units - those in fireflies flashing in unison, neurons discharging together, and social groups forming together. Our results show that the variability of interaction processes can be accurately described by a two-parameter model, which combines an exponential distribution and an inverse Gaussian distribution. This accurate description enables us to accurately predict the behavior of the system at different scales of observation, from a few connected units to the entire meta-population, based on local interaction parameters, the network's structure, and the chosen variation measurement. This accurate prediction has significant implications for understanding and studying self-sustaining population units, whether they are fireflies, neurons, or social groups.

Recently, actor-critic reinforcement learning has achieved notable success in a variety of applications, but traditional actor-critic methods face a common challenge: they typically employ gradient descent for parameter updates, which limits their performance in high-dimensional continuous state and action spaces. This limitation can be particularly problematic when dealing with models characterized by strong local structures. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach, called maximization-acceluated actor-critic (MAXAC), which leverages Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) to perform efficient parameter updates on both the actor-critic network and the policy. The MAXAC method integrates time-evolution dynamics from the HMC into the policy-network update process, thereby enhancing its exploration capabilities. Our research demonstrates the maximization of the expected Q-value and the likelihood ratio test under the time-evolution policy, yielding improved performance in both on- and off-line settings. When compared to state-of-the-art actor-critic methods, our MAXAC approach showcases superior performance, particularly in high-dimensional continuous state and action spaces.

Basic number theory shows that for any natural number n, there is a prime number that can be expressed in the form of nx + a, where 0 less than or equal to x, and a is a natural number less than or equal to n factorial. This proof leads to the conclusion that there are infinitely many prime numbers. It also demonstrates that for any natural number n, there are at least two prime numbers of the form p, where n less than or equal to p, and p is a prime number, with the difference between the two prime numbers being less than 2n, thus proving the Twin Prime Conjecture.

Achieving stable flight in UAVs is complicated by the absence of a direct position reference. A novel solution proposed involves the use of layered navigation with real-time acoustic sonar integration to guide UAVs toward their targets. This research focuses on the real-time sonar data acquisition and resolution, crucial components for the navigation controller to function effectively. A specific sonar device was tested and demonstrated the required performance, yielding acceptable position estimates suitable for control purposes. The performance evaluation utilized a controlled outdoor setup and the results confirmed the feasibility of this approach.

The only two confirmed moons of Neptune, Nereid and Prospero, exhibit unique characteristics.  While Prospero is a small, close-orbiting irregular satellite, Nereid is a larger, more distant moon with an unusual, highly elliptical orbit.  Unlike other Neptune moons that are composed of water ice, rock, and tholin, Nereid's surface is distinct.  Despite its water ice spectral features, it lacks the red color of other moons and instead displays red features at wavelengths of 1.5 and 2.0 micrometers.  By analyzing Nereid's reflectance spectrum in the near-infrared range, it is determined that the red color on its surface is not uniform, but a combination of red and blue-colored materials.  Water ice is present in varying states, but it is not the red-colored substance, and it is hypothesized that the red color could be derived from dark, blue-colored water ice or an alternative material.  The findings also suggest that the red color could be a thin layer of water ice on top of a different, red-colored material, and that the red features are consistent with a water ice layer of a specific thickness.  The research also considers the possibility of other red-colored materials, such as iron oxide or complex organic molecules, but the red color of the surface is not fully explained. We build projective lines from a specific type of matrix ring, then use this to define the projective and affine planes. 
Our method proves that if a set of matrices over a division ring is a subring of the full $3 \times 3$ matrix ring, it's isomorphic to a different set of matrices. 
This result allows us to conclude that the projective plane built from this set is the same as the one defined by the Freudenthal-Hesse normal form. 
Similarly, our process shows the corresponding equivalence of related affine planes.

We establish the exact conditions for when one model of set theory is Tukey-order greater than another model, by examining Pawlikowski's principles of idealization. Specifically, we determine for which pairs of regular cardinals and initial ideals their associated principles idealize one set greater than the other. This investigation also reveals novel applications and properties of idealization, expanding upon previous work by Cichoń and Tukey.

A new objective function called negativity in operations research seeks to minimize the highest possible regret. In this work, we explore its application to Bayesian dynamic treatment regimes. To achieve optimal policies under negativity in an unknown environment, we develop a Bayesian online learning approach based on UCB algorithms. A key theoretical finding shows that the regret incurred by this approach grows at the same rate as the best fully known policy would have experienced. Additionally, we validate its performance through extensive opUCB simulations and real-world tests on patient decision-making.

This article explores key concepts in duality theory, particularly those related to topological spaces and modules with various topological properties. It introduces novel types of spaces, such as HA-spaces and RE-spaces, with modified topologies derived from original spaces. A new class of topological modules, influenced by Wilker's work, is considered. The study focuses on properties like compactness, boundedness, projectivity, injectivity, and duality for modules. The investigation includes generating dualities for a range of homogeneous spaces and applying them to establish equivalences between categories of modules with different topological properties. Additionally, applications to homological principles are discussed.

A recent inquiry by Spekkens proposed redefining local realism by utilizing a complexified version of the $E_8$ symmetry, and demonstrating that this inquirer's position holds substantial merit. To explore whether the inquirer's position leads to local hidden variable theories, we have constructed a 248-dimensional Hilbert space and developed an 84-inquirer, 248-answer quantum-like experiment based on a 168-element group, which is a component of the $E_8$ symmetry. The results of our analysis show that the inquirer's position leads to local hidden variable theory failure, and furthermore, the results show a failure of WITS contextuality, a milder form of contextuality. The 84 questions asked in the experiment are 84-inquirers, and the experiment involves 248 answers, which are made up of 7-tuples of values (±1). The inquirer's questions and answers rely on a 168-element group, which is defined by a 5-element, 12-element, and 28-element subgroups, and the inquirer's questions and answers show the inquirer's position leads to a contextuality-related failure, and the inquirer's position is confirmed to be contextually-related.

We investigate superconductivity in systems with many-body interactions from a microscopic perspective. Our analysis reveals that superconductivity in topological systems can be attributed to the presence of specific singularities, known 'soft modes', and a topological property that characterizes these topological materials. To address this finding, we propose a general principle stating that if the conditions for a given ground state are characterized by 'soft modes' and topological properties, then fluctuations of the order parameter in topological superconductors will demonstrate an enhanced response. Based on this principle, we observe that superconductivity in topological systems with many-body interactions is preferentially **s**-wave rather than **p**-wave. Our theoretical predictions for topological superconductivity can potentially be verified through the observation of fractional excitations and the emergence of Kondo effects in this class of superconductors.

We have generalized Polya's classic theorem, which stated that if the circle is represented by a set of topological generators, then the set is actually algebraically and topologically isomorphic to the circle. This idea has been further extended to linked groups in our approach. Specifically, we consider the quotient group $G/H$, where $G$ is a topological group and $H$ a closed subgroup. If the homology groups of $G$ in dimensions 0 and 1 are identical to those of $H$ and certain additional conditions on the compactness and locally contractible properties of both groups are met, then $G$ and $H$ share the same continuity properties. Furthermore, if both groups are also of dimension 1 and satisfy specific homology and compactness rules, then $G$ and $H$ are both algebraically and topologically isomorphic.

Presence-absence data, characterized by a preponderance of zero values, are prevalent in numerous scientific domains. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of various clustering techniques tailored to handle sparse data, incorporating both established methods and a new approach called Sparse PCA-based K-Means. The effectiveness of these algorithms is demonstrated on both artificial and genuine sparse datasets, with a focus on accuracy and computational efficiency. The integration of Sparse PCA-based K-Means yields improved accuracy compared to traditional K-Means, particularly when combined with PCA for dimensionality reduction. Notably, this method excels in dealing with sparse data, outperforming PCA+SDCA+K-Means in terms of accuracy, particularly when employing 2-component clustering.

In vision tasks, salient objects are frequently identified within images that have multiple colors and depth information. Although many approaches exist for recognizing prominent objects in monochromatic, tri-chromatic, and depth-enhanced images, there is no single method capable of handling all these variations. This study proposes a comprehensive and efficient salient object detection approach that works on both RGB and RGB+D images. By exploiting the extra information provided by depth data, our technique takes advantage of additional image cues to identify the most prominent objects. Through extensive testing on various benchmark datasets, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance in several advanced salient object detection evaluations.

The UM-IU@LING system for the fifth aggressive language assessment is based on two primary components: classifying English tweets as aggressive or not, and explaining the reasons for such classification. This system employs two models: a BERT-based model that predicts tweet aggression and a linear support vector machine classifier that analyzes BERT output, tweet text, and user profile information to determine the aggression level. The BERT model is also utilized to generate reasons for classifying non-aggressive tweets as such. Evaluations demonstrate that this system achieves a F1 score of 0.7032 on the test dataset for single-label classification and a F1 score of 0.7002 for multi-label classification.

A number is considered palindromic in base $b$ if its base-$b$ representation is a palindrome. We identify a critical difference between the quotients of two palindrome quotients conjectures based on whether the base $b$ is composite or not. Our analysis reveals all possible quartets of integers $(x, x/q, p_1, p_2)$ where the base $b$ representation of $x/q$ is a proper palindrome quotient with weight $w=p_1$ and length $w+p_2=p_2=b+2$, given that the greatest common divisor of $x$ and $q$ equals $1$. Furthermore, for bases $b$ that are prime and $q$ being $2$ or greater, the base $b$ representation of $x/q$ is a proper palindrome quotient with weight $w$, and its shifted version is a $2$-nonpalindrome with the same weight and length. A significant finding is that this applies to a vast number of palindrome quotient bases $b_q$ for $q$ being prime and $b_q$ being a primitive root of $q$, especially as these bases increase.

Computed tomography (CT) imaging systems are limited by various factors, such as different X-ray energies, noise from detectors, and the inability to visualize certain materials. To overcome these constraints, we developed an advanced reconstruction method that simultaneously addresses these issues. This innovative approach formulates a CT reconstruction problem as a variational model, taking into account system limitations, measurement noise, and the unique properties of various polyenergetic materials. Solved using the alternating direction method of multipliers, our algorithm produces high-quality CT reconstructions, accurate material maps, and an estimate of the CT image, all while minimizing the effects of noise and the initial system limitations.

Historically, handwritten text recognition tasks have relied on large, carefully curated datasets for training, but recent advancements in generation techniques allow for the creation of diverse training data from a single dataset, and in this work, a new method is proposed, which utilizes a template-based approach to create realistic character samples for hand-written text recognition. The generated data outperforms existing synthetic data and significantly improves state-of-the-art models on handwritten character recognition, particularly on datasets with limited resources, while also enabling the pre-training of models using the generated data for fine-tuning on real data.

Heavy superconducting nuclei, particularly those near the N=120 closed shell, hold significant interest for theoretical and experimental research. The occurrence of novel phenomena in this area, such as isomeric gamma-softness and strange deformation, has been suggested in previous studies. The present work involves merged ab initio calculations to investigate the nature of these nuclei. Specifically, the authors combined the findings from two different methods, the Green's function Goldstone many-body perturbation theory and the coupled cluster approach, to compute the single-particle energies of selected heavy nuclei. The study utilized a novel, effective, low-momentum potential to facilitate the merging of these calculations, and the results demonstrate excellent convergence for selected semimagic nuclei. For specific reactive nuclei such as $^{154}$Dy and $^{162}$Dy, the authors found low-spin ground-state band structures that exhibited characteristics of isomeric gamma-softness and strange deformation. The nature of these reactive nuclei was then analyzed by examining their Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov mean-field properties. The study found that the low-energy excited states in these nuclei were well reproduced by a quasiparticle random phase approximation on top of the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov ground state.

To begin understanding the SSH model, we suggest starting with its one-dimensional version. The model's simplicity lies in alternating hopping amplitudes between even and odd sites, leading to different topological phases depending on these amplitudes. The topological nature of a phase can be confirmed through the presence of edge states at a given energy, while one-dimensional topological phases are fully described by Chern numbers. This can be extended to two dimensions by considering coupled SSH chains, forming a BHZ model, and calculating relevant topological invariants like the Chern number and orbital magnetization. The latter can be enhanced through a time-periodic drive and calculated using microscopical or gauge-orbital approaches.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with specific compact domains in C^n, particularly those shaped like squares, balls, and other convex regions. Also investigated are composition operators in A_2(B), where B represents the boundary of an domain, and a specific area, D, bounded by a circle and a parabola.

We utilize the two-loop R-rigid superspace two-theorem to demonstrate that the four-point on-shell amplitude in supersymmetric QCD, where all external legs have the same spin and helicity, is finite. This proof confirms the finiteness conjecture for N=4 super-Yang-Mills theory. The proof leverages the equivalence between two-loop R-rigid superspace amplitudes and combinations of two-loop NHM (non-holomorphic) and NHM-like amplitudes in N=4 super-Yang-Mills theory. The proof further establishes that the sum of these amplitudes is single-valued, is singly-valent under super-Witt reparametrizations, and exhibits specific transformation properties under the spin group. High-performance programming on GPUs is typically achieved through custom, low-level memory management techniques, such as using the host device to allocate and manage memory pools for devices. However, these methods require significant modifications to the programmers' code and do not support high-level programming languages that rely on memory allocation APIs. In this research, a new GPU object-oriented memory allocation algorithm is developed to bridge this performance gap, and can be integrated into a compiler to enhance the performance of C++/CUDA code written on GPUs. This novel algorithm partitions memory into multiple pools, and uses a data structure to track each pool's fragmentation status, and dynamically assigns the most suitable pool size for each memory request to minimize fragmentation. By offloading memory management tasks to the compiler, High-level programming languages can achieve significant performance improvements without requiring modifications to the original code, and outperforms existing solutions by reducing memory allocation time, overhead, and reducing fragmentation.

A variety of minimal $U(1)$ models have been proposed to address physics beyond the Standard Model, with the simplest models being the most frequently examined. This work explores the characteristics of the extra $U(1)$ models derived from $E_6$ and $SO(10)$ grand unified theories, with a focus on the phenomenology of the simplest models. By calculating the couplings of the models, the most likely values for the mixing angle between the models and a method for distinguishing the models based on these parameters are established. Additionally, the potential for distinguishing the models through their impact on Higgs-Higgs-Z-Z interactions at particle colliders is investigated, with significant model-dependent differences found between the models. By combining constraints from flavor physics, dark matter, and the electroweak precision, a likelihood region in the parameter space of the models is identified, with the most probable values of the mixing angle between the models lying between approximately $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-2}$. A detailed comparison with the simplest model is provided, with the model exhibiting greater compatibility with current data due to its larger value for the mixing angle between the models.

Understanding the cane industry's production process, researchers studied the mechanical behavior of cane tubes. The investigation revealed that, despite the complexity of cane's internal structure, the laws of mechanics can effectively explain its mechanical properties. A theoretical model was developed to compute the cane tube's longitudinal tension and circumferential strain under pressure, accounting for the thin-shell effect. This computation enabled calculation of the cane bundle's elastic properties, showing that the modulus of elasticity for Indian cane is consistent with values used in engineering designs. The study also found that the modulus of elasticity is five times lower than the modulus of rigidity. The interaction between cane fibers was modeled, considering the radial expansion of the cane when pressurized, which affects the cane's longitudinal tension and explains the cane's mechanical stability under pressure. The theoretical model's predictions matched the observations made during the mechanical tests conducted on the cane tubes.

In safety-critical applications, ensuring that systems are reliable is essential. This importance is particularly heightened when considering that many systems are complex and cannot be fully understood. To address this issue, a concept known as robustness assurance has emerged, allowing engineers to quantify a system's reliability without needing full knowledge of its underlying model. This paper explores an efficient method for computing robustness assurance by representing Bayesian networks using probabilistic circuits and formulating an optimization problem. To enhance computational performance, a simplified version of this problem is proposed by relaxing the constraints imposed by the Markov property. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments.

Researchers have developed a method to observe Bloch oscillations in an acoustic waveguide made of acoustic metamaterial. The principle underlying this demonstration relies on the interaction between sound waves and a periodically structured medium. By introducing a frequency-modulated pulse of acoustic energy into this material, the team successfully observed the back-reflection of the pulse, which is a direct result of the Bloch oscillations. The acoustic metamaterial used in this study was designed to have unique properties that allow for the manipulation of sound waves. These properties are based on the mathematical description of these materials as having both positive and negative effective mass. The observation of Bloch oscillations in ultrasonics opens up new possibilities for the manipulation of high-frequency acoustic waves.

This research focuses on classifying the Neighbour-Transitive codes, a specific subset of codes with symmetrical properties within generalised quadrangles. These codes will be shown to encompass existing NT codes and extendable to new forms. Furthermore, geometry and group theory applications of NT codes were explored. Geometrically, NT codes correspond to configurations of subspaces in generalised quadrangles with uniform intersection patterns. An analysis of potential automorphism group actions on NT codes was conducted, confirming their maximality in certain quadrangles and identifying instances of maximal subgroups generating new NT codes in the quadrangle of type $Q(5, q)$ for odd $q$.

To quantify an anisotropic spatial distribution, a two-dimensional correlation function has been developed and demonstrated using the dense molecular cloud data from the GCMS survey of the GCML. This new approach offers distinct advantages over traditional trispectrum methods by providing ease of implementation, ease of interpretation, and ease of comparison across multiple datasets. These benefits stem from its focus on 2D patterns, its straightforward 360-degree symmetry application, and its straightforward scaling of two-dimensional bin sizes. When applied to GCML, this framework successfully identified the elongated patterns and dense molecular cloud alignment along the NE-SW axis and revealed additional rectilinear patterns aligned with the major axes of the GCML. Furthermore, this method can easily quantify and account for anisotropic measurement uncertainties.

To analyze electron creation following nonlinear X-ray absorption, a simple model is developed and applied to simulate the absorption near-edge spectra of germanium at high energies. This is achieved by similing the temporal evolution of electron groups based on electron creation rate and energy. Two simple shapes of electron energy distributions were assumed, and calculations of absorption near-edge spectra were conducted by similing electron contributions via their core holes and valence holes at these energies. This model effectively reproduces the significant changes in absorption near-edge spectra observed experimentally at high X-ray pulse energies, particularly at the absorption threshold and due to core hole screening.

A proposed temperature sensing system uses a body effect-based MOSFCTA buffer current generator and an embedded on-chip bandgap reference to achieve temperature measurements within a wide voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V. The temperature sensing system employs single-ended sigma-delta modulators and an embedded on-chip two's complement digital-to-analog converter with an integrated digital buffer and negative feedback loop to improve conversion speed and accuracy. Temperature measurements are conditioned by a proposed switched-capacitor low-pass filter and converted to an analog output signal via a 12-bit voltage-controlled integrand-controlled switched-capacitor amplifier. The analog output can be converted to a temperature value via a proposed on-chip 12-bit current-mode ADC. The system employs open-loop and closed-loop single-ended switched-capacitor amplifiers to enhance performance, power efficiency, and area. The temperature sensing system employs a proposed on-chip hysteresis comparator and an embedded on-chip 0.6V bandgap reference to improve robustness.
