This paper explores active learning techniques to improve robot localization and mapping capabilities. We propose a novel approach that combines active prediction with deep learning methods to create an efficient and accurate robot navigation system. The framework uses a compact neural network to predict key points in a robot's path, allowing it to adapt to various environments. The size of the environment influences the number of predicted points, and our approach outperforms traditional full path prediction methods in terms of accuracy and processing efficiency. Simulation studies demonstrate the value of active learning in terms of reduced training data requirements and better error propagation compared to conventional methods. The findings suggest that active learning can contribute to the development of autonomous navigation systems, even though further research is needed to translate these predictions into actionable control strategies.

At high-energy physics conferences, raw data from experiments is showcased in video form, allowing researchers to track the progress of individual events. However, the immense size of the data captured by the experiment, particularly in 3D sparse formats, poses a challenge. Current data compression techniques are ineffective for such data, leading to a need for a more suitable solution. This paper suggests an innovative approach, utilizing a specialized autoencoder that can efficiently compress 3D sparse data. By leveraging a dual-convolution strategy, both on the original and compressed data, the proposed method yields high-quality results at various compression rates. Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) has demonstrated remarkable success in sparsifying the data from a Time Projection Chamber (TPC), with an average compression rate of 30.66%, significantly outperforming existing techniques that achieve only 4.82% compression.

We analyze the finizy gravity model, where gravitational interaction decreases at large distances, and generate and examine the evolution of artificial universes containing clusters. The resulting distributions of cluster sizes and spacing show good agreement with the finizy model, unlike in general relativity, where such structures do not develop. Instead, the finizy model yields a stable hierarchical arrangement of unispherical bodies across various length scales. We also compare the size distribution of clusters in the finizy model with observed galactic clusters, finding comparable patterns in both datasets.

A geometric hypergraph can be defined by associating each vertex with a point in d-dimensional space, where the edges consist of collinear sets of vertices. Researchers have been interested in the minimum number, denoted as f(d), required to create a convex 3-partite hypergraph with part sizes n and where every edge contains at least three points, where it saturates by removing any vertex from it. In this paper, we show that there exists a sequence of such convex 3-partite saturation instances that increase without bound and approach the total number of vertices, namely 2dn, which notably surpasses previously known saturation instances and relates to a long-standing open problem in d-dimensional geometry.

To investigate the structure of compound nuclei formed in $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V collisions at lower energies, an alpha cluster string model was employed in this research. By incorporating relativistic projectile and target cluster wave functions, this model accurately accounts for the excitation of both the projectile and target nuclei. Calculated cross sections for $\alpha$ production in breakup and fusion-evaporation reactions were compared with experimental results, which provided a clear distinction between the two processes. This model also predicted angular distributions for the $\alpha$ particles in both breakup and fusion-evaporation reactions, which can be utilized to determine the primary energy range for $\alpha$ generation in experiments.

This study presents a closed-loop vision-based controller for the Pacific Lamprey-inspired robotic swimmer PILS, capable of navigating complex environments. The PILS model features two rotating degrees of freedom and is designed to replicate the swimming motion of a Pacific Lamprey. The controller utilizes a learned swim cycle and closed-loop feedback to maintain stable gait and progress forward through various challenges, including flow and obstacles. By integrating model prediction and feedback correction, the controller ensures consistent progression and enables the PILS to climb vertical surfaces and navigate around obstacles. The controller relies on a simple, feed-forward neural network that predicts body angles and generates optimal stroke parameters. The PILS controller demonstrates a significant improvement in swimming efficiency and stability when using feedback compared to open-loop control. The successful navigation of the PACMAN obstacle course by the PILS robot, which features a rotating fin, validates the effectiveness of the new controller in controlling complex systems.

This study presents a theoretical framework for optimizing treatments in diseases that impact the immune system. Focusing on colon cancer, which interacts with the immune system in complex ways, T-cell therapies have emerged as a promising treatment. To address the variability in patient responses and the limited understanding of these interactions, this framework employs the Fokker-Planck framework. It incorporates observed data into a probabilistic model, which is then used to optimize the dosage and frequency of anti-CTLA4 and anti-PD-1 antibody treatments. By incorporating a Bayesian approach, this framework enables treatments to be tailored to individual patient needs. In simulations, treatments using this framework resulted in higher T-cell levels and better colon cancer clearance. This framework holds potential for enhancing the effectiveness of current T-cell therapies in the future.

In Device-to-Device communication, minimizing the age of data exchange is a top priority for efficient operations. In a scenario where Data Communication Blocks form virtual pairs through a two-dimensional spatial arrangement, we introduce a novel age of information (AoI) metric for each DCB pair and give rise to the age of convergence, a novel metric that measures the average age of all DCB pairs at steady state. To minimize the age of convergence, we define an optimization problem involving the placement of DCB pairs and develop an associated computational issue. By analyzing the problem's structure, we discover that its solution yields both optimal ordering and pairing strategies, corresponding to the solution of a linear assignment problem. To address this linear assignment problem, we propose a policy iteration approach, backed by theoretical proofs of bounded increments, and integrate reinforcement learning to accelerate its convergence using past experiences of DCB formation. Simulations demonstrate that this formulation effectively results in lower age of convergence compared to existing formation policies.

This research focuses on verifying that certain solutions of the barotropic Euler equations in three-dimensional space maintain their helicity. The helicity conservation is essentially a symmetry property that arises from a specific mathematical equation, which can be seen as a passive scalar advection equation. This theory is a core component of fluid dynamics. The verification process involves two key aspects: first, confirming that the solution initially possesses the required symmetry, and second, proving that the numerical discretization accurately models the symmetric nature of the equations, thereby ensuring that the solution remains consistent with the theoretical predictions.

This paper investigates the reflection coefficient of the four-dimensional linear Schrödinger equation modified by a potential, referred to as the DSI equation. A solution to this coefficient is expressed in terms of the Fourier transform of the initial conditions. We find that the reflection coefficient's magnitude is bounded by $|k|^{-3}$ at large values of $|k|$, while a specific example illustrates that this bound cannot be improved upon.

Current gravitational-wave detectors primarily measure the overall shape of co-orbiting binary systems, but they can also determine their orbital orientation and distance, albeit with varying precision along the binary's path. For the first time, a series of calculations precisely estimates the residual orbital distortion of inspiralling binaries at GW detection thresholds, taking into account different types of stars and distances. These estimates will aid in understanding the limitations and improvements of future detectors, as well as the reconstruction of binary system parameters by full orbital models beyond the scope of this work.

A new type of X-ray amplifier fueled by an x-fre electron laser is being explored, 
where a small number of electrons generate massive amounts of coherent X-rays. 
In this modified amplifier configuration, a free-electron laser is integrated, 
replacing one of its standard components, to enable the amplification of X-rays 
with high brightness. The idea involves using a gain medium that is not present 
at the free-electron laser's operating wavelength, allowing the X-rays from the 
lasor to interact with the medium and stimulate the emission of even more X-rays. 
This innovative approach has the potential to significantly enhance the performance 
of existing free-electron laser technology and produce even more intense X-rays.

Dynamic graph incidents like sudden changes in social networks can have significant effects. Research has been conducted on detecting incidents in static or evolving graphs, but real-world networks change gradually. This paper assumes a real-world dynamic graph that gradually evolves and develops new connections. Using a mean-field game approach, the paper develops an algorithm that identifies incidents in a dynamic graph that evolves in real-time and predicts future connections. The proposed algorithm is tested on two synthetic scenarios and one actual Facebook connection dataset.

High-energy astrophysical phenomena, such as supernovae and gamma-ray bursts, are widely believed to originate from massive stellar core collapse. These events involve the formation of an accretion shock that drives the system and emits energy. Researchers have studied this accretion shock for decades, focusing on its behavior and stability. Recent discoveries have revealed that the nature of the shock may be determined by a critical threshold related to the Lewis number. This is particularly relevant for ionic DSA, which requires a radiatively inefficient and time-stable accretion shock. This work investigates the stability of the accretion shock by examining its convergence and resolution methods, revealing that all numerical resolutions converge to the correct Einstein-Scharzschild self-similar solution except for a critical minimum upstream density. It is shown that a total variation diminishing scheme accurately reproduces the self-similar profile, while other numerical methods fail and develop unphysical oscillations. Downstream, a critical minimum upstream density corresponds to the Lewis number threshold. This critical minimum density represents the transition point where the shock transitions from stable to unstable. This research highlights the importance of considering varying density effects in studying accretion shocks and their implications for high-energy astrophysical phenomena.

The growing interest in AI and increasing public scrutiny have led many organizations to integrate the development of explainable AI as part of their AI projects. However, there is still limited guidance on how to effectively communicate the need for clear AI explanations to users. To address this gap, we have conducted an initial investigation into making AI explanations more comprehensible, with the ultimate goal of uncovering the user's understanding requirements. This was done by gathering input from 23 stakeholders across three separate workshops. As a result, we have produced a initial model specifying user-centered explainability requirements for various scenarios, as well as a framework to guide engineers in specifying how to make AI explanations more understandable to users. This model also provides a set of suggestions, such as implementing user tests, to verify that the explanations meet user requirements. This paper shares our findings and provides the basis for exploring other make AI more understandable related topics, with the ultimate goal of making the AI more accessible to users.

The analysis of histopathological slides plays a significant role in numerous medical diagnoses and disease prognoses made by medical professionals. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to notable achievements in disease classification and organ segmentation from histopathological slides. However, the development of such models is often hindered by the limited availability of large, annotated histopathological datasets. In response to this challenge, the first authors from the University of Torino have created a dataset named UniToPatho. This dataset comprises 1527 H&E stained microscopic fields, each examined by two pathologists who provided detailed annotations on the polyp's adenoma abnormality. The dataset will serve as a valuable resource for researchers in the computer-aided diagnosis field.

In the context of zero-error information theory, we explore how side information can influence coding rates beyond the traditional mutual information limit. While past research has identified the conditional entropy of typical sets as a critical factor, we take a different approach by examining the graph representing possible source outcomes and conditionally available side information. This graph-based analysis leads to a more nuanced understanding, and we provide a specific single-pass coding method with a new lower bound on its performance. This bound, though not yet proven to be universally tight, helps to quantify the gap between single-pass and multi-pass coding efficiency. The size of this gap is influenced by the structure of the graph and side information, and we use specific examples to demonstrate its potential limitations.

A new deep generative model, a modified Hogsline-Ahmed-Romanovski (HAR)隐式正则化框架，is introduced in this research and adapted to tackle the challenge of enhancing SAR images. The original HAR framework integrated a Markov random field and an autoencoder to facilitate SAR enhancement, but its performance was limited by a simplistic prior and an inefficient search algorithm for the Markov random field, which hindered its applicability to real-world SAR images. To address these shortcomings, a new term combining a hierarchical prior and a neural network is added to the HAR framework, which serves as the new deep generative model, a modified HAR framework. The proposed model, MrSARP, is found to significantly outperform the existing methods in multiple simulated and actual SAR enhancement scenarios.

A recent advancement in near-term quantum computing is the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), which aims to solve complex NP optimization problems. Effective QAOA performance depends on choosing the right parameters in its variational cycle. Traditionally, optimizing these parameters has been challenging, requiring access to a quantum device and often yielding poor results. To address this, a novel approach is introduced that utilizes Bayesian optimization to automatically determine the parameters. By breaking down the search for optimal parameters into hierarchical layers, this method reduces the complexity and facilitates better convergence. Experimental results from IQM's 32-qubit quantum processor along with simulations indicate that this method outperforms other approaches in qubit-efficient processors but may struggle with deeper circuits due to noise.

A precise, versatile formula has been developed for determining the area where parts of ellipses overlap. This mathematical proof is based on exact calculus and holds true for any arrangement of ellipses in space and their orientation. The created algorithm efficiently computes the intersection area by adapting to different scenarios and breaking down complex polygons into triangular sections, which can then be used to calculate the area of ellipses, even when only partially present, and their intersections.

Reinforcement learning is a fundamental concept in decision-making under uncertainty, where agents learn to make the best possible choices by exploring their surroundings and retaining the most valuable knowledge. A key technique in reinforcement learning is the q-learning algorithm, a type of dynamic programming that enables agents to learn optimal policies without needing a model of their environment. Over time, this algorithm has been refined for various scenarios, such as bounded scenarios, infinite horizons, and continuous time, to accommodate real-world applications outside the realm of classic tabular settings. This paper presents a new version of the q-learning algorithm designed for continuous duration scenarios, where time is measured in real numbers. This novel algorithm incorporates a time discretization that adapts to the learning process, and comes with strong theoretical guarantees, such as convergence to a fixed point and sub-optimality bounds that depend on the smoothing of the action values. These results demonstrate that the algorithm can effectively learn even when the optimal policy is unknown or non-stationary.

Our research, conducted on the Hubbard model for triangular lattices with repulsive interactions, reveals that antiferromagnetic ordering emerges when a small portion of the lattice is occupied by holes doping a half-filled system. When this hole doping exceeds a certain threshold, the magnetic structure transforms into a helical pattern. In the absence of hole doping and with a certain parameter setting, we discovered that the system's ground state exhibits 120-degree symmetry, yet thermal fluctuations cause it to evolve into a six-fold pattern. This is the first instance where such a phenomenon has been observed in a triangular lattice without the influence of long-range interactions. Our findings are supported by a combination of variational cluster expansion and quantum Monte Carlo techniques.

Accurately identifying and numbering the vertebrae in spinal CT scans is a complex task that current deep learning methods struggle to achieve completely. This problem can be exacerbated by the similarities between vertebrae and the transformations that occur between different coordinate systems. This paper introduces an innovative approach that incorporates a image rectification step and an anatomically-informed optimization strategy to streamline automatic vertebrae localization and identification. By incorporating constraints related to the first and last vertebrae, an optimization strategy is developed to ensure accurate vertebrae segmentation and numbering while maintaining anatomical plausibility and facilitating efficient convergence. This approach is validated through comprehensive experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness in various clinical settings and coordinate system orientations, and is made available for download.

In stochastic thermodynamics, electrical currents are typically conserved due to the network's symmetry. This research focuses on the general case where conductance matrices aren't symmetric, resulting in fluctuating currents that deviate from defined paths. We start by standardizing the statistics of these fluctuating currents as time steps approach zero, utilizing a continuous limit and a gauge-invariant formulation. This limits statistics are then generalized to multicomponent systems, and an entropy production framework is proposed that is valid for multicomponent gauge-invariant scenarios.

We examine how quantum cohomology changes in relative settings when algebraic varieties undergo specific transformations, focusing on both quantized versions of relative symplectic structures and K-stability. This analysis yields both previously known and new formulas for relative quantum structures, which in turn enable an innovative approach to constructing relative quantum Gromov-Witten polynomials. Additionally, it supports the hypothesis that relative quantum structures maintain consistency for these specific transformations.

This study explores atomic-level sound wave transfer between two piezoelectric aluminum nano-cystals held in vacuum by an atomic force microscope. The experiments reveal that sound waves can be fully transmitted from one crystal to another despite the extreme fineness of the connection, with no loss of energy. The connection's mechanical properties match theoretical expectations, explaining the phenomenon of full energy transfer. This finding contrasts with previous assumptions that large crystals would have minimal effect on microscopic objects. The phenomenon may have significant implications for creating advanced sound-isolating technologies and particle-based computing systems.

A novel approach, reservoir photonics, has gained significant attention in the study of non-equilibrium systems due to its simplicity and effectiveness. This method, which utilizes a thermal reservoir instead of traditional cold-atom systems, has demonstrated success in a range of applications, including mode-competition and spatial pattern formation. This review explores recent advancements in reservoir photonics, focusing on experiments with exciton-polariton condensates. This setup, consisting of a microcavity laser above a semiconductor substrate, offers an efficient and flexible research platform. Our discussion covers both one- and multi-component systems, and we highlight new possibilities for dynamic systems, as well as novel applications, and output devices based on reservoir photonics.

The presence of exoplanetary dust disks beyond the main sequence stars has been extensively documented. Despite this, details of the corresponding mass loss processes are still shrouded in mystery. Research on the hot Jupiter K2-22 b yielded contradictory conclusions regarding its temperature and atmospheric properties. This study presents the most definitive evidence to date of large dust particles in a nearby evaporating exoplanet, as demonstrated by low-resolution spectroscopic observations of circumstellar emission conducted with the Large Binocular Telescope. Analysis of the shape of the continuum and dust features indicates a substantial mass loss rate of the exoplanet at approximately 7.3 x 10exp(-4) expMearth per million years. This data highlights the necessity of further mid-infrared spectroscopic studies of evaporating exoplanets to further refine our understanding of mass loss and dust particle size distributions.

We establish a strong form of the topological Milnor fiber theorem for holomorphic map germs with non-degenerate critical points, combining elements of Pdloss and Marar's work with Newton's polygon methods and Narkiewicz's patching technique. This leads to a new, simpler proof that the $m$-jet space of the germ is flat over the $m$-dimensional base space, effectively showing that the projection from the $m$-jet space to Jet$^m$(C, C) is a flat morphism. Furthermore, the result enables the extension of the Milnor fiber to a family of flat map germs defined over an affine space.

The rise of Big Data has led to a pressing need for advanced data analysis tools.
In this paper, we introduce Daany, an open-source C# library designed for data
analysis and visualization, allowing users to work with various data formats
including relational, network, and JSON. Daany's rich set of features enables
comprehensive data exploration, pattern detection, and efficient query
formulation. It also integrates C#'s type safety to enhance development
speed and ensure correctness.

This study argues that the scientific revolution was driven by mathematics rather than reasoning, as evidenced by Galileo's adoption of Aristotelian principles of motion. By the 17th century, mathematics had evolved into a theoretical framework that could generate predictions. This new approach to mathematics led Galileo to reject traditional principles of motion and embrace his own theory, which was later validated by Newton's laws. This discovery challenges the long-standing view that the scientific revolution was a gradual process of using empirical evidence to refine theories, as demonstrated by Galileo's reliance on existing principles of motion. This study suggests that the scientific revolution was actually characterized by sudden shifts between distinct theories, as theories were chosen based on their mathematical basis rather than their empirical evidence. This implies that the scientific revolution was more about the power of mathematics to generate predictions than it was about the power of reasoning.

To investigate the impact of non-standard radiation from the Early Universe, we developed an equation of state that takes into consideration the effects of Relic Neutrinos and Dark Matter. This impact is further amplified by the Saha's ionization process, which results in a unique state of photons that deviates from a standard blackbody distribution, particularly at lower frequencies. We also examined how the impact of Dark Energy modifies this photon distribution, which is initially influenced by the spherically symmetric distribution of the Early Universe.

The merging of magnetic fields, known as magnetic island coalescence, is a process that's still not fully understood in the complex behavior of plasmas. To study this phenomenon, we used a two-part model. The model combines a fluid-based simulation with a particle-based simulation. The fluid model, based on resistive magnetohydrodynamics, is combined with an adaptive model of particle-in-cell to capture kinetic effects at magnetic reconnection sites. The simulation, run on a supercomputer, involved two different adaptively embedded particle-in-cell domains to investigate early and late-stage magnetic reconnection. A programmer's assistant, known as a coding assistant, helps developers by offering suggestions for potential code modifications and can also create complete code snippets at a developer's request. The code snippets provided by a coding assistant are referred to as snippets. A pioneering approach to building such an assistant is called Amanuensis, a method where the assistant is trained on existing code bases to learn how skilled programmers write their code. Once trained, Amanuensis can be prompted by a developer to write code, and when prompted, it generates both the code and an accompanying description of the code, based on the description given by the developer. Unlike other methods, Amanuensis only uses existing code as training data. Although this approach has many benefits, it also has some drawbacks. One of the main challenges of using Amanuensis is managing long snippets, as they can be very complex and difficult to understand. Another difficulty lies in accurately describing the code, as even the original programmer may have a hard time explaining their code, let alone an artificial assistant. Despite these challenges, Amanuensis has shown promising results, and researchers are actively exploring ways to make it work more effectively.
